readings.title: Little Bo-Peep
readings.challenge: Follow a lost-and-found story told in five short verses.
readings.focus: A shepherdess’s worry, dream and search end in a comic surprise about the sheep’s tails.
readings.context: Bo-Peep is a shepherdess, a girl who looks after sheep. A crook is a shepherd’s hooked stick; bleating is the sound sheep make; fleeting means running away; espied means saw; hillocks are little hills. Old rhymes like this one enjoy a silly ending.

excerpt.locator: “LITTLE BO-PEEP,” the complete rhyme; opens “Little Bo-Peep has lost her sheep, And can't tell where to find them; Leave them alone,…”; closes “…tried what she could, as a shepherdess should, That each tail should be properly placed.”.

questions.prompt: What advice does the first verse give about the lost sheep?
facilitatorNotes: Leave them alone and they will come home, bringing their tails behind them. Ask whether the advice turns out right: the sheep do come back, but not as expected.
evidence: Leave them alone, and they'll come home,
And bring their tails behind them.

questions.prompt: What did Bo-Peep dream, and what did she find when she woke?
facilitatorNotes: She dreamt she heard them bleating, but awake she found them still running away, so the dream was a joke on her.
evidence: And dreamt she heard them bleating;
For still they all were fleeting.

questions.prompt: What has happened to the sheep’s tails, and what does Bo-Peep try to do about it?
facilitatorNotes: The sheep left their tails hanging on a tree to dry, and she tries to put each one back where it belongs. Children may find this funny or sad; Bo-Peep sighs and wipes her eye, so both feelings fit.
evidence: All hung on a tree to dry.
That each tail should be properly placed.

readings.title: Little Boy Blue
readings.challenge: Hear a problem, a question and a surprising answer in four lines.
readings.focus: The animals have wandered off because the boy who should watch them is asleep.
readings.context: A horn is an animal’s horn blown to make a loud call. Corn here means a field of grain, where a cow should not be. A haystack is a big pile of dried grass. Read the last line in a whisper.

excerpt.locator: “LITTLE BOY BLUE,” the complete rhyme; opens “Little Boy Blue, come, blow your horn! The sheep's in the meadow, the cow's in the corn.…”; closes “…corn. Where's the little boy that looks after the sheep? Under the haystack, fast asleep!”.

questions.prompt: Where are the sheep and the cow, and where should they be?
facilitatorNotes: The sheep are in the meadow and the cow is in the corn, eating the grain; both should be in their own field. That is why someone needs to blow the horn.
evidence: The sheep's in the meadow, the cow's in the corn.

questions.prompt: Who is supposed to look after the sheep, and where is he?
facilitatorNotes: Little Boy Blue, fast asleep under the haystack.
evidence: Where's the little boy that looks after the sheep?
Under the haystack, fast asleep!

questions.prompt: What should he do with his horn? Would you wake him, and how?
facilitatorNotes: Blow it to call the animals back. Children can choose to wake him gently or let him sleep; the rhyme does not say what happens next.
evidence: Little Boy Blue, come, blow your horn!

readings.title: Three Children on the Ice
readings.challenge: Hear a rhyme that is partly a joke and partly a warning.
readings.focus: A comic old warning about ice ends with advice to parents that turns back on itself.
readings.context: Long ago children slid on frozen ponds in winter. “Upon a summer’s day” is a joke, because ice melts in summer. “The rest they ran away” means the others ran off. “Ten thousand pounds to one penny” means almost certainly. Abroad means out of the house.
readings.contentNote: Three children fall through the ice and drown; the rhyme treats it lightly, as a warning.

excerpt.locator: “THREE CHILDREN ON THE ICE,” the complete rhyme; opens “Three children sliding on the ice Upon a summer's day, As it fell out, they all fell in,…”; closes “…ye, too, who have none, If you would keep them safe abroad Pray keep them safe at home.”.

questions.prompt: What were the three children doing, and on what kind of day?
facilitatorNotes: Sliding on the ice on a summer’s day. Ask what is silly about that: ice does not stay frozen in summer.
evidence: Three children sliding on the ice
Upon a summer's day,

questions.prompt: Where does the rhyme say they should have been instead?
facilitatorNotes: At school, or sliding on dry ground, where they could not fall in.
evidence: Oh, had these children been at school,
Or sliding on dry ground,

questions.prompt: The last verse talks to parents. What does it tell them?
facilitatorNotes: To keep their children safe at home if they want them safe outside: a joke, since staying home means not going out at all. It can lead to a real talk about keeping safe near ice and water.
evidence: If you would keep them safe abroad
Pray keep them safe at home.

readings.title: Going to St. Ives
readings.challenge: Listen to a riddle carefully enough to catch its trick.
readings.focus: A counting riddle piles up sevens, but the answer depends on who was going which way.
readings.context: St. Ives is a town in England. A sack is a big bag; kits are kittens. This rhyme is a riddle, so read it twice: once for fun and once to listen for the trick.

excerpt.locator: “GOING TO ST. IVES,” the complete rhyme; opens “As I was going to St. Ives I met a man with seven wives. Every wife had seven sacks,…”; closes “…Every cat had seven kits. Kits, cats, sacks, and wives, How many were going to St. Ives?”.

questions.prompt: Who does the speaker meet on the way to St. Ives?
facilitatorNotes: A man with seven wives. Long ago, riddles liked big surprising numbers.
evidence: I met a man with seven wives.

questions.prompt: What is in each sack, and what does each cat have?
facilitatorNotes: Seven cats in every sack, and seven kittens for every cat. Children can hold up seven fingers for each step.
evidence: Every sack had seven cats,
Every cat had seven kits.

questions.prompt: How many were going to St. Ives? Listen again to the first line before you answer.
facilitatorNotes: The trick answer is one, the speaker, because the others were met coming the other way. Some people answer with a huge number, since the rhyme does not say which way the man was walking; a child who notices that is also listening well.
evidence: As I was going to St. Ives
How many were going to St. Ives?

readings.title: When Jenny Wren Was Young
readings.challenge: Follow a proposal and an answer that says yes to one thing and no to another.
readings.focus: Robin offers Jenny fine food and fine clothes; she takes Robin but keeps her plain brown dress.
readings.context: Jenny Wren, a small brown bird, and Robin Redbreast are a pair in many old rhymes. Gallant means brave and polite; doffed his hat means took it off to greet her; to appoint the day means to choose the wedding day. Currant wine is a drink made from small berries; goldfinches and peacocks are brightly coloured birds; a gown is a dress. Give Robin a grand voice and Jenny a firm one.

excerpt.locator: “WHEN JENNY WREN WAS YOUNG,” the complete rhyme; opens “'Twas once upon a time, when Jenny Wren was young, So daintily she danced and so prettily…”; closes “…nice and so is currant wine, But I must wear my plain brown gown and never go too fine."”.

questions.prompt: What does Robin promise Jenny if she will marry him?
facilitatorNotes: Cherry pie, new currant wine, and fine clothes that would make her look like a goldfinch or a peacock.
evidence: You shall feed on cherry pie and drink new currant wine,
I'll dress you like a goldfinch or any peacock gay,

questions.prompt: What does Jenny say yes to, and what does she say no to?
facilitatorNotes: Yes to Robin, because she loves him; no to the fine clothes, because she will keep her plain brown gown.
evidence: Since, dearest Bob, I love you well, I'll take your offer kind.
But I must wear my plain brown gown and never go too fine.

questions.prompt: Why might a wren want to keep her plain brown gown?
facilitatorNotes: Real wrens are small brown birds, so the gown is simply what she is; she may like herself as she is, or not want to show off. Children may also say brown is easier to keep clean, which the rhyme does not say but does not rule out.
evidence: But I must wear my plain brown gown and never go too fine.

readings.title: Simple Simon
readings.challenge: Hear a string of short adventures that all go wrong in the same way.
readings.focus: Each of Simon’s plans fails because he has not thought about how things really work.
readings.context: Simple here means foolish. A pieman sold pies at fairs, and his ware is what he sells. A thistle is a prickly weed. People once joked that you could catch a bird by putting salt on its tail. A sieve is a bowl full of holes for draining. Adieu means goodbye.

excerpt.locator: “SIMPLE SIMON,” the complete rhyme; opens “Simple Simon met a pieman, Going to the fair; Says Simple Simon to the pieman, "Let me…”; closes “…with a sieve, But soon it ran all through; And now poor Simple Simon Bids you all adieu.”.

questions.prompt: Why won’t the pieman let Simon taste a pie?
facilitatorNotes: Simon has no penny, and the pieman wants to be paid first.
evidence: "Show me first your penny,"
"Indeed, I have not any."

questions.prompt: Where does Simon go fishing for a whale?
facilitatorNotes: In his mother’s pail, which is far too small. Children can show with their arms how big a whale is and how big a pail is.
evidence: For to catch a whale;
Was in his mother's pail!

questions.prompt: Which of Simon’s mistakes is the silliest? Tell why.
facilitatorNotes: Any choice works if the child says what Simon forgot: plums do not grow on thistles, salt will not catch a bird, and water runs out of a sieve. The question asks for a reason, not one right answer.
evidence: If plums grew on a thistle;
He went for water with a sieve,

readings.title: Humpty Dumpty
readings.challenge: Work out what someone is from what happens to him.
readings.focus: A rhyme that began as a riddle: something that falls and can never be put back together.
readings.context: The rhyme never says what Humpty Dumpty is. Long ago it was a riddle, and its answer was an egg, which is why pictures show him that way. The King’s men are his soldiers.

excerpt.locator: “HUMPTY DUMPTY,” the complete rhyme; opens “Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall, Humpty Dumpty had a great fall; All the King's horses, and…”; closes “…All the King's horses, and all the King's men Cannot put Humpty Dumpty together again.”.

questions.prompt: Where was Humpty Dumpty sitting, and what happened?
facilitatorNotes: On a wall, and he had a great fall.
evidence: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall,
Humpty Dumpty had a great fall;

questions.prompt: Who came to help him?
facilitatorNotes: All the King’s horses and all the King’s men. Ask whether horses could really help.
evidence: All the King's horses, and all the King's men

questions.prompt: Why can’t they put him together again? What do you think Humpty Dumpty is?
facilitatorNotes: He has broken, and nobody can mend him. An egg fits the clue, since a cracked egg cannot be put back; children may suggest other breakable things, which is how riddles work.
evidence: Cannot put Humpty Dumpty together again.

readings.title: Old Mother Hubbard
readings.challenge: Keep track of a long pattern: each time she goes out, the dog is doing something new.
readings.focus: A tireless old woman runs errands for a dog who keeps surprising her, until they part with polite bows.
readings.context: This rhyme is a joke in which a dog does impossible human things. Tripe is a cheap meat; an undertaker arranges funerals; an alehouse and a tavern sell drinks; the hatter, barber, fruiterer, tailor, cobbler (shoemaker), sempster (sewer of linen) and hosier (seller of stockings) all keep shops. A curtsy and a bow are polite greetings.
readings.contentNote: The dog seems to be dead and is then found laughing; he is also fetched beer and smokes a pipe. These are comic touches in an old rhyme.

excerpt.locator: “OLD MOTHER HUBBARD,” the complete rhyme; opens “Old Mother Hubbard Went to the cupboard, To give her poor dog a bone; But when she got…”; closes “…a curtsy, The dog made a bow; The dame said, "Your servant," The dog said, "Bow-wow."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the poor dog get no bone at the start?
facilitatorNotes: The cupboard is bare. The whole rhyme grows out of that empty cupboard.
evidence: The cupboard was bare,
And so the poor dog had none.

questions.prompt: Choose one shop Mother Hubbard visits. What is the dog doing when she comes back?
facilitatorNotes: Any matching pair counts, such as the barber’s and dancing a jig, or the cobbler’s and reading the news. Children can act out the dog’s trick.
evidence: He was dancing a jig.
He was reading the news.

questions.prompt: How do the dame and the dog say goodbye, and what is funny about the dog’s answer?
facilitatorNotes: She curtsies and he bows, and she says “Your servant,” a polite greeting. He answers “Bow-wow”: after behaving like a person all through the rhyme, he still talks like a dog.
evidence: The dog made a bow;
The dog said, "Bow-wow."

readings.title: Jack and Jill
readings.challenge: Follow a short story to its second verse, which many people never hear.
readings.focus: A tumble down the hill is followed by an old-fashioned cure.
readings.context: A pail is a bucket. Jack’s crown is the top of his head, and so is his nob. To caper is to skip. Dame Dob is an old woman; long ago, vinegar and brown paper were put on bumps to soothe them.

excerpt.locator: “JACK AND JILL,” the complete rhyme (two verses); opens “Jack and Jill went up the hill, To fetch a pail of water; Jack fell down, and broke his…”; closes “…as he could caper, To old Dame Dob, who patched his nob With vinegar and brown paper.”.

questions.prompt: Why did Jack and Jill go up the hill?
facilitatorNotes: To fetch a pail of water. Long ago many families carried their water from a well or spring.
evidence: To fetch a pail of water;

questions.prompt: What happened to Jack, and then to Jill?
facilitatorNotes: Jack fell down and hurt his head, and Jill came tumbling after him.
evidence: Jack fell down, and broke his crown,
And Jill came tumbling after.

questions.prompt: How did Dame Dob fix Jack’s head? What might we use today?
facilitatorNotes: She patched it with vinegar and brown paper. Today we might use ice, a plaster or a doctor. The second verse makes the story end happily, since Jack trots off quickly.
evidence: As fast as he could caper,
With vinegar and brown paper.

readings.title: If All the Seas Were One Sea
readings.challenge: Build bigger and bigger things in your mind, then hear what happens when they meet.
readings.focus: A rhyme makes four enormous things and brings them together for one giant splash.
readings.context: An axe is a tool for chopping down trees. The words printed in slanting letters (great, that) are meant to be said with extra weight. Make each “great” sound bigger than the last, and save your biggest voice for the splash.

excerpt.locator: “IF ALL THE SEAS WERE ONE SEA,” the complete rhyme; opens “If all the seas were one sea, What a _great_ sea that would be! And if all the trees were…”; closes “…_great_ tree, And let it fall into the _great_ sea, What a splish splash _that_ would be!”.

questions.prompt: Name the four great things the rhyme imagines.
facilitatorNotes: A great sea, a great tree, a great axe and a great man. Children can stretch their arms wider for each one.
evidence: If all the seas were one sea,
And if all the men were one man,

questions.prompt: What does the great man do with the great axe?
facilitatorNotes: He cuts down the great tree and lets it fall into the great sea.
evidence: And cut down the _great_ tree,
And let it fall into the _great_ sea,

questions.prompt: How big would that splash be? Why does the rhyme save it for the very end?
facilitatorNotes: Bigger than any real splash, because everything in it is the biggest of all. Every line has been building up to it, so the last line pays off the whole rhyme. Let the child make the splash.
evidence: What a splish splash _that_ would be!

readings.title: Baa, Baa, Black Sheep
readings.challenge: Hear a question and an answer, and work out who gets the wool.
readings.focus: A sheep shares out three bags of wool, and one little boy gets none.
readings.context: Wool is the soft hair cut from a sheep and spun into yarn for clothes. “Yes, marry, have I” is an old way of saying “Yes indeed, I have.” A master and a dame are the man and woman in charge of a house or farm; a lane is a narrow country road. Ask the question in one voice and let the child answer as the sheep.

excerpt.locator: “BAA, BAA, BLACK SHEEP,” the complete rhyme; opens “Baa, baa, black sheep, Have you any wool? Yes, marry, have I, Three bags full;”; closes “One for my master, One for my dame, But none for the little boy Who cries in the lane.”.

questions.prompt: How much wool does the black sheep have?
facilitatorNotes: Three bags full.
evidence: Three bags full;

questions.prompt: Who gets the bags of wool?
facilitatorNotes: One goes to the master and one to the dame, but none to the little boy in the lane.
evidence: One for my master,
But none for the little boy

questions.prompt: Why do you think the little boy gets none? Is that fair?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme does not say. Children may guess he gets none because he is crying, or because the wool is not his; some will say it is unfair. Many people know another version in which the little boy down the lane gets a bag; this book’s version leaves him out.
evidence: But none for the little boy
Who cries in the lane.

readings.title: The Cat and the Fiddle
readings.challenge: Enjoy nonsense: things that could never happen.
readings.focus: A rhyme of impossible pictures, with a little dog laughing at them just as listeners do.
readings.context: A fiddle is a violin. “Hey, diddle, diddle” is nonsense sound to start the fun. Sport means fun or a game. Read it with a bounce, and let the child join the last line.

excerpt.locator: “THE CAT AND THE FIDDLE,” the complete rhyme (“Hey, diddle, diddle!”); opens “Hey, diddle, diddle! The cat and the fiddle, The cow jumped over the moon; The little dog…”; closes “…the moon; The little dog laughed To see such sport, And the dish ran away with the spoon.”.

questions.prompt: What does the cow do?
facilitatorNotes: Jumps over the moon. Children can show how high that is.
evidence: The cow jumped over the moon;

questions.prompt: Why does the little dog laugh?
facilitatorNotes: Because it is such fun to watch. The dog laughs at the silliness, just as we do.
evidence: The little dog laughed
To see such sport,

questions.prompt: Which things in the rhyme could never really happen? Which one is the silliest?
facilitatorNotes: A cat with a fiddle, a cow over the moon, a laughing dog, a dish running away with a spoon. Any choice is right if the child can say why it is silly.
evidence: The cat and the fiddle,
And the dish ran away with the spoon.

readings.title: Sing a Song of Sixpence
readings.challenge: Keep track of who is where in a royal household.
readings.focus: A surprising pie starts a rhyme that visits the king, the queen and the maid, and ends with a peck.
readings.context: A sixpence was a small coin; rye is a grain; four-and-twenty means twenty-four. Dainty means special and good to eat. A counting-house is a room for counting money; a parlor is a sitting room.
readings.contentNote: A blackbird snaps off the maid’s nose; old rhymes like this one enjoy a sudden comic ending.

excerpt.locator: “SING A SONG OF SIXPENCE,” the complete rhyme; opens “Sing a song of sixpence, A pocket full of rye; Four-and-twenty blackbirds Baked in a pie!”; closes “…the garden, Hanging out the clothes; When down came a blackbird And snapped off her nose.”.

questions.prompt: What was baked in the pie, and what happened when it was opened?
facilitatorNotes: Twenty-four blackbirds, and they began to sing. Ask whether that is a real recipe; it is a royal surprise.
evidence: Four-and-twenty blackbirds
The birds began to sing;

questions.prompt: Where are the king, the queen and the maid, and what is each one doing?
facilitatorNotes: The king counts money in his counting-house, the queen eats bread and honey in the parlor, and the maid hangs out the clothes in the garden.
evidence: The king was in his counting-house,
Eating bread and honey.

questions.prompt: What happens to the maid at the end? Why might a blackbird do that?
facilitatorNotes: A blackbird swoops down and snaps off her nose. Perhaps it is one of the pie birds, cross at being baked; the rhyme does not say, so children can guess.
evidence: When down came a blackbird
And snapped off her nose.

readings.title: The Mulberry Bush
readings.challenge: Act out each verse as it is read or sung.
readings.focus: A singing game keeps the same tune and changes the action in every verse.
readings.context: This is a game song: children hold hands and go round in a ring for the first verse, then act out each action. A mulberry bush is a bush with dark berries. Sing or chant it with the actions, and let the child join in the repeated words.

excerpt.locator: “THE MULBERRY BUSH,” the complete rhyme; opens “Here we go round the mulberry bush, The mulberry bush, the mulberry bush, Here we go…”; closes “…come out of school, This is the way we come out of school, On a cold and frosty morning.”.

questions.prompt: What jobs do the singers act out?
facilitatorNotes: Washing hands, washing clothes, going to school and coming out of school. Children can show each one.
evidence: This is the way we wash our hands,
This is the way we wash our clothes,

questions.prompt: Which line comes back at the end of every verse? What kind of morning is it?
facilitatorNotes: “On a cold and frosty morning”: a chilly morning with frost on the ground. Ask what the children might be wearing.
evidence: On a cold and frosty morning.

questions.prompt: Show how you go to school and how you come out of school. Why might they look different?
facilitatorNotes: The rhyme only names the actions, so children choose: some walk slowly in and run out happily, others walk in eagerly. Any action they can explain fits.
evidence: This is the way we go to school,
This is the way we come out of school,

readings.title: The House That Jack Built
readings.challenge: Remember a chain that grows one link longer with every verse.
readings.focus: Each new verse adds one character, so the whole chain must be said again, all the way back to the house.
readings.context: Malt is grain kept for brewing; worried means bit and shook; forlorn means sad and lonely; tattered and torn means in ragged clothes; shaven and shorn describes a priest with a shaved head, as some priests had long ago. Let the child join in on the repeated lines, and go a little faster as the chain grows.
readings.contentNote: The cat kills the rat and the dog worries the cat, as animals do.

excerpt.locator: “THE HOUSE THAT JACK BUILT,” the complete rhyme; opens “This is the house that Jack built. This is the malt That lay in the house that Jack built.”; closes “…the cat, That killed the rat, That ate the malt That lay in the house that Jack built.”.

questions.prompt: What does the cow with the crumpled horn do to the dog?
facilitatorNotes: She tosses it, flinging it up with her horns. Children can show a gentle toss with their hands.
evidence: This is the cow with the crumpled horn,
That tossed the dog,

questions.prompt: Who is added last of all, and what does he do?
facilitatorNotes: The farmer sowing the corn, who keeps the cock that crowed in the morn. Ask how far back the chain goes from him: all the way to the house.
evidence: This is the farmer sowing the corn,
That kept the cock that crowed in the morn,

questions.prompt: Every verse ends with the same line. Why do you think the rhyme keeps going back to the house?
facilitatorNotes: Everything in the chain happens in or near Jack’s house, so it always ends where it began. A child who notices that every verse gets longer has found the other half of the pattern.
evidence: That lay in the house that Jack built.

readings.title: Little Jenny Wren
readings.challenge: Follow a friendship that changes once one bird gets better.
readings.focus: Robin looks after Jenny while she is sick; once she is well she says she does not love him, and he scolds her.
readings.context: Jenny Wren, a small brown bird, and Robin Redbreast are a pair in many old rhymes. “Upon a time” means once; “You shall be mine” means “I will be your sweetheart.” “Out upon you” and “Fie upon you” are old ways of saying “Shame on you.”
readings.contentNote: An angry Robin calls Jenny an old insulting name, “Bold-faced jig,” meaning a rude, flighty girl.

excerpt.locator: “LITTLE JENNY WREN,” the complete rhyme; opens “Little Jenny Wren fell sick, Upon a time; In came Robin Redbreast And brought her cake…”; closes “…being angry, Hopped upon a twig, Saying, "Out upon you! Fie upon you! Bold-faced jig!"”.

questions.prompt: What does Robin bring Jenny when she is sick?
facilitatorNotes: Cake and wine, and he tells her to eat and drink well.
evidence: And brought her cake and wine.

questions.prompt: What does Jenny promise while she is sick, and what does she tell Robin when she is well?
facilitatorNotes: She promises “You shall be mine,” but once she is up she says plainly that she does not love him at all.
evidence: You shall be mine.
She loved him not a bit.

questions.prompt: How does Robin feel at the end? Did either bird behave well?
facilitatorNotes: He is angry, hops onto a twig and scolds her. Children may say Jenny broke her promise, or that Robin should not call names; both use the text. Some may think Jenny was right to be honest.
evidence: Robin being angry,
Bold-faced jig!

readings.title: I Saw a Ship A-Sailing
readings.challenge: Picture a make-believe ship from its cargo to its captain.
readings.focus: A ship of treasures, sailed by mice and captained by a duck, is imagined as a gift for the listener.
readings.context: Comfits are small sweets; the cabin is a room on a ship; the hold is the space below deck for cargo; laden means loaded. A packet is a bundle. Read the captain’s last words with gusto.

excerpt.locator: “I SAW A SHIP A-SAILING,” the complete rhyme; opens “I saw a ship a-sailing, A-sailing on the sea; And, oh! it was all laden With pretty…”; closes “…a packet on his back; And when the ship began to move, The captain said, "Quack! Quack!"”.

questions.prompt: Who is the ship full of pretty things for?
facilitatorNotes: “For thee”: for you, the listener. Ask how it feels to be the one the ship is coming for.
evidence: With pretty things for thee!

questions.prompt: What are the sails and masts made of?
facilitatorNotes: Silk sails and golden masts, far finer than any real ship’s.
evidence: The sails were made of silk,
And the masts were made of gold.

questions.prompt: Who are the sailors and who is the captain? How can you tell this is a make-believe ship?
facilitatorNotes: Twenty-four white mice and a duck who says “Quack! Quack!” Animal sailors, silk sails and golden masts all show it is make-believe; any one of these is good evidence.
evidence: Were four-and-twenty white mice
The captain was a duck,

readings.title: Old King Cole
readings.challenge: Hear a list of three, and a song inside a song.
readings.focus: A cheerful king calls for his comforts and his music, and the rhyme says no one can match him.
readings.context: A merry old soul is a cheerful old person. His pipe was for smoking and his bowl held a drink. Fiddlers play fiddles, or violins. Rare means wonderful. Let the child sing the fiddlers’ line.

excerpt.locator: “OLD KING COLE,” the complete rhyme; opens “Old King Cole Was a merry old soul, And a merry old soul was he; He called for his pipe,…”; closes “…fiddlers. Oh, there's none so rare As can compare With King Cole and his fiddlers three.”.

questions.prompt: What three things does King Cole call for?
facilitatorNotes: His pipe, his bowl and his three fiddlers.
evidence: He called for his pipe,
And he called for his fiddlers three!

questions.prompt: What sound do the fiddles make?
facilitatorNotes: “Twee tweedle dee, tweedle dee.” Children can hum or sing it.
evidence: "Twee tweedle dee, tweedle dee," went the fiddlers.

questions.prompt: What kind of king is Old King Cole? Which words tell you?
facilitatorNotes: A merry, cheerful one who loves music; the rhyme says nobody can compare with him and his fiddlers. Children may say he is jolly, happy or musical.
evidence: Was a merry old soul,
With King Cole and his fiddlers three.

readings.title: A Week of Birthdays
readings.challenge: Match each day of the week with what the rhyme says about children born on it.
readings.focus: An old fortune-telling rhyme gives each day of birth a different kind of child.
readings.context: This old rhyme pretends to tell what a child will be like from the day of the week he or she was born. Fair of face means good-looking; grace means gentle beauty; woe means sadness; to work hard for a living means to work hard to earn money. The Sabbath day here is Sunday; bonny and blithe mean pretty and cheerful, and gay means merry. If you know the day your child was born, say it before you read.

excerpt.locator: “A WEEK OF BIRTHDAYS,” the complete rhyme; opens “Monday's child is fair of face, Tuesday's child is full of grace, Wednesday's child is…”; closes “…But the child that's born on the Sabbath day Is bonny and blithe, and good and gay.”.

questions.prompt: What does the rhyme say about Monday’s child and Sunday’s child?
facilitatorNotes: Monday’s child is good-looking; Sunday’s child is pretty, cheerful, good and merry.
evidence: Monday's child is fair of face,
Is bonny and blithe, and good and gay.

questions.prompt: Which day sounds the saddest? Which sounds the busiest?
facilitatorNotes: Wednesday is “full of woe,” the saddest; Saturday “works hard for its living,” the busiest. Thursday’s child, with “far to go,” may also sound tiring.
evidence: Wednesday's child is full of woe,
Saturday's child works hard for its living,

questions.prompt: Can the day you were born really decide what you are like? Why might people enjoy the rhyme anyway?
facilitatorNotes: No; it is a game, and the words were chosen partly to rhyme (woe and go). People enjoy finding their own day and comparing. A child born on a Wednesday can be as happy as anyone.
evidence: Thursday's child has far to go,

readings.title: For Want of a Nail
readings.challenge: Follow a chain of losses from the smallest thing to the biggest.
readings.focus: One tiny missing nail leads, step by step, to the loss of a whole kingdom.
readings.context: “For want of” means because something was missing. Long ago soldiers rode horses into battle, and a horseshoe was held on with small nails. Read slowly so each step can be heard, and let the child count the steps on their fingers.

excerpt.locator: “FOR WANT OF A NAIL,” the complete rhyme; opens “For want of a nail, the shoe was lost; For want of the shoe, the horse was lost; For want…”; closes “…For want of the battle, the kingdom was lost, And all for the want of a horseshoe nail.”.

questions.prompt: What was lost first, and why?
facilitatorNotes: The horse’s shoe, because a nail was missing.
evidence: For want of a nail, the shoe was lost;

questions.prompt: What is lost at the very end? Count the steps to get there.
facilitatorNotes: The kingdom. The steps run shoe, horse, rider, battle, kingdom: five losses from one nail.
evidence: For want of the battle, the kingdom was lost,

questions.prompt: What could someone learn from this rhyme?
facilitatorNotes: That small things can matter a great deal, so they are worth taking care of. Children may say it in their own words or give an example from life, kept separate from the rhyme.
evidence: And all for the want of a horseshoe nail.

readings.title: The Bells
readings.challenge: Hear church bells talk to each other, one after another.
readings.focus: The bells of London churches argue about money that is owed, then simply ring out lists of things.
readings.context: London has many old churches, each with its own bells, and this rhyme gives each church’s bells words that rhyme with its name (St. Helen’s and shillings, Old Bailey and pay me). Shillings, halfpence and farthings were English coins; brickbats are broken bricks; pokers and tongs are fireplace tools. Read it like bells answering each other, some high and some low.

excerpt.locator: “THE BELLS,” the complete rhyme; opens “"You owe me five shillings," Say the bells of St. Helen's. "When will you pay me?" Say…”; closes “…slippers," Say the bells of St. Peter's. "Pokers and tongs," Say the bells of St. John's.”.

questions.prompt: What do the bells of St. Helen's say, and what do the bells of Old Bailey ask?
facilitatorNotes: St. Helen’s says, “You owe me five shillings,” and Old Bailey asks, “When will you pay me?”
evidence: You owe me five shillings,
When will you pay me?

questions.prompt: When will the money be paid? What does the great Bell of Bow say?
facilitatorNotes: “When I grow rich,” and when will that be? The great Bell of Bow says, “I do not know,” so perhaps never.
evidence: When I grow rich,
I do not know,

questions.prompt: After Bow, the bells stop talking about money. What do they say instead, and why might the rhyme end that way?
facilitatorNotes: Lists of things, kettles and pans, old shoes, pokers and tongs, each chosen to rhyme with a church’s name. The argument turns into the sound of bells ringing. Some children may say the bells are offering things instead of money.
evidence: Kettles and pans,
Pokers and tongs,

readings.title: London Bridge
readings.challenge: Hear each building plan and the reason it fails.
readings.focus: The rhyme tries one material after another until stone at last will hold.
readings.context: London Bridge crosses the River Thames, and the old bridges there were damaged more than once. “Dance over my Lady Lee” and “With a gay lady” are singing lines from a game; gay here means merry. Stole means stolen; huzza means hooray.

excerpt.locator: “LONDON BRIDGE,” the complete rhyme; opens “London Bridge is broken down, Dance over my Lady Lee; London Bridge is broken down, With…”; closes “…so strong, Dance over my Lady Lee; Huzza! 'twill last for ages long, With a gay lady.”.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with London Bridge at the start?
facilitatorNotes: It is broken down, so the song asks how to build it up again.
evidence: London Bridge is broken down,
How shall we build it up again?

questions.prompt: Why won’t silver and gold do? Why won’t iron and steel?
facilitatorNotes: Silver and gold will be stolen; iron and steel will bend and bow. Each material has its own problem.
evidence: Silver and gold will be stole away,
Iron and steel will bend and bow,

questions.prompt: What do they build with at last, and how long will it last?
facilitatorNotes: Stone so strong, which will last for ages. Ask whether the child agrees that stone is best and why; another idea is fair if it is kept separate from the rhyme.
evidence: Build it up with stone so strong,
Huzza! 'twill last for ages long,

readings.title: Ding, Dong, Bell
readings.challenge: Sort out who harmed the cat and who helped her.
readings.focus: A rhyme tells of a cruel trick and a rescue, and says plainly whose side it is on.
readings.context: A well is a deep hole with water at the bottom, from which people drew water in a bucket. A barn is a farm building where grain was stored, which mice like to eat, so a cat that caught them helped the farmer. “Ding, dong, bell” is the sound of a bell ringing, as if to raise the alarm.
readings.contentNote: A boy puts a cat in a well to drown her; another boy pulls her out, and the rhyme calls the first boy naughty.

excerpt.locator: “DING, DONG, BELL,” the complete rhyme; opens “Ding, dong, bell, Pussy's in the well! Who put her in? Little Tommy Lin.”; closes “…poor pussy-cat. Who never did him any harm, But killed the mice in his father's barn!”.

questions.prompt: Who put the cat in the well, and who pulled her out?
facilitatorNotes: Little Tommy Lin put her in; Little Johnny Stout pulled her out.
evidence: Little Tommy Lin.
Little Johnny Stout.

questions.prompt: What does the rhyme call the boy who tried to drown the cat?
facilitatorNotes: A naughty boy; the rhyme takes the cat’s side.
evidence: What a naughty boy was that,

questions.prompt: The rhyme says the cat “never did him any harm.” What good had she done? Why does the rhyme tell us?
facilitatorNotes: She killed the mice in his own father’s barn, so she was helping his family. That makes his trick unfair as well as cruel.
evidence: Who never did him any harm,
But killed the mice in his father's barn!

readings.title: The Death and Burial of Poor Cock Robin
readings.challenge: Match each creature to the job it takes on.
readings.focus: Creatures answer one question after another until every task is done and all the birds mourn Cock Robin.
readings.context: Each answer in this old rhyme rhymes with the creature’s name. A shroud is a cloth wrapped round someone who has died; a clerk and a parson help lead a church service; a psalm is a sung prayer; to toll a bell is to ring it slowly when someone dies; a kite is a bird of prey; the chief mourner is the one who grieves most.
readings.contentNote: A sparrow shoots Cock Robin with a bow and arrow, and the rhyme names his blood, his grave and his funeral.

excerpt.locator: “THE DEATH AND BURIAL OF POOR COCK ROBIN,” the complete rhyme; opens “Who killed Cock Robin? "I," said the sparrow, "With my little bow and arrow, I killed…”; closes “…of the air Fell sighing and sobbing, When they heard the bell toll For poor Cock Robin.”.

questions.prompt: Who killed Cock Robin, and with what?
facilitatorNotes: The sparrow, with his little bow and arrow.
evidence: "I," said the sparrow,
"With my little bow and arrow,

questions.prompt: Pick a creature. What job does it do, and what word rhymes with its name?
facilitatorNotes: For example, the owl digs the grave “with my spade and trowel,” and the bull tolls the bell “because I can pull.” Let the child hear each name and its rhyme.
evidence: "I," said the owl,
"Because I can pull,

questions.prompt: How do the birds feel when the bell tolls? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: Sad: they fall sighing and sobbing, and the dove mourns for her love. Ask whether the sparrow is sorry too; the rhyme does not say, so any answer is a guess.
evidence: Fell sighing and sobbing,
"I mourn for my love,
